item.title: ChatGPT Slides has Shipped, but on Windows 10 the Desktop App Gives You a PowerPoint File (3 minute read)
item.description: ChatGPT Slides began rolling out on October 16 to Pro, Business, and Enterprise users with Space access, but the Windows 10 desktop app provides a PowerPoint file instead of a collaborative deck. Decks live inside Space and inherit its view-and-edit sharing, with ChatGPT joining in when @mentioned like a colleague. Exports reach PowerPoint, PDF, or Google Slides, while Free, Go, and Plus plans still have no release date.

item.title: Google Search Tests Layout Change For Local Knowledge Panel (1 minute read)
item.description: Google is testing a redesigned local knowledge panel that moves the business name, rating, description, and action buttons above the photos, bringing desktop results closer to the existing mobile design. The lower section has also been tightened to create a more compact overall layout. The changes are subtle but could affect how prominently actions such as calls, directions, and website visits appear to searchers.

item.title: Apple's ‘Designers of Tomorrow' highlights creative projects from emerging designers (3 minute read)
item.description: Apple and Design Miami's second Designers of Tomorrow showcase features work from Salem S. Charabi, Isabel Rower, Yoonjeong Lee, and Parafernalia centered on the theme of presence. Their projects explore how physical objects can capture attention and shape experiences, ranging from lighting and furniture to pieces designed for shared interaction. Apple devices are integrated throughout their creative processes, including MacBook Pro for 3D modeling, iPad Pro and Apple Pencil for sketching, and iPhone, Procreate, FaceTime, and iCloud for documenting and collaborating remotely.

item.title: Design System Foundations (2 minute read)
item.description: Any team producing designed outputs already has a design system, which turns the work into incremental improvement rather than a build from zero. Before excitement takes over, everyone needs to agree whether the system means a component library, a shared Figma file, or documentation. Starting with color and typography distilled from existing practice gives guardrails, not straitjackets, and avoids the objections that come with imposed rules.

item.title: A founder with a tool is not a founder with a clue (22 minute read)
item.description: AI has dramatically lowered the cost of producing software, allowing solo founders to handle work that previously required designers, engineers, and other specialists, but easier production does not automatically provide the expertise required to judge whether the result is good. Product quality still depends on hard-earned understanding of users, trust, interaction, strategy, and countless subtle decisions that generative tools can execute without truly evaluating. Small AI-enabled teams can be extraordinarily effective, but treating specialist expertise as unnecessary confuses the ability to make something with the ability to recognize, shape, and refine something worth making.

item.title: Don't Prompt AI. Delegate to It (4 minute read)
item.description: Prompting is fading as a personal skill, and a weekend-built Jira and Confluence briefing agent shows the alternative: letting AI write the prompt while a human defines what good looks like. Four or five rewrite rounds produced a prompt that groups tickets by business topic, flags unverifiable claims, and obeys one key line: do not invent facts. Research backs the approach, with LLM-written instructions matching or beating human ones on 19 of 24 tasks in the 2022 APE paper.

item.title: Review AI-Generated UI Changes with Storybook and Chromatic (8 minute read)
item.description: Sprawling AI-generated UI changesets can pass linting yet render broken layouts, which makes raw diff review structurally inadequate. A four-step playbook scopes each prompt to a single component, isolates changes in Storybook, automates visual regression with Chromatic, and adds a PR checklist. Together they close the gap between code that compiles and code that renders correctly.

item.title: Debunking AI Agent Accessibility Claims and Solving AI Alignment for Accessibility (7 minute read)
item.description: Agents routinely claim work they never did, and having one agent validate another is like letting the fox guard the henhouse. Deque's report found that 88 percent of engineering leaders trust their AI-generated code is accessible, while 64 percent cite accessibility as a top driver of rework. A deterministic harness asking AI only narrow yes-or-no questions creates proof-of-work records for human verification, with Deque reporting that a 30-to-45-minute keyboard test can take seconds.

item.title: The State of Typography in Design Systems (8 minute read)
item.description: A survey of 94 UX and product designers found that 78% can easily change or suggest fonts, while brand alignment is the leading consideration when choosing typefaces, followed by accessibility. Most design systems use fewer than 10 typographic styles, potentially too few to cover common needs, while token adoption remains inconsistent and decisions about typography are rarely revisited after implementation. Scaling type across screen sizes and choosing appropriate styles emerged as the biggest challenges, alongside maintaining cross-platform consistency and getting developers and stakeholders to support better typographic decisions.

item.title: For a brief generation or two, we clicked (2 minute read)
item.description: Graphical interfaces made clicking and tapping a temporary language humans had to learn to communicate with computers, while conversational AI may return interaction to the far older and more natural behavior of simply saying what we want.

item.title: The Senior Art Director Behind Assassin's Creed's Visual Identity Shares His Personal Sketches (1 minute read)
item.description: Montreal art director Raphaël Lacoste, who shaped Assassin's Creed's visual identity at Ubisoft, shares personal sketches and monumental landscape paintings that echo 19th-century Romantic painters like Caspar David Friedrich.

item.title: Gemini Notebook Adds Review before Generating Slides and Videos (1 minute read)
item.description: Gemini Notebook now lets users review a slide outline or video producer notes and request changes before anything renders. With the optional Review toggle on in the Studio panel, users can ask for edits like an executive summary or reordered scenes, then select Proceed. Google announced the update on October 19 and is rolling it out globally to all users over the following week.

item.title: Why we refreshed the n8n brand (4 minute read)
item.description: n8n has refreshed its identity with a new logo, typeface, and refined color system to reflect its evolution from workflow automation into a platform for building interconnected workflows and AI agents. The new mark shifts attention from connected nodes themselves toward the activity happening between them, while the typography balances technical precision with the human character of n8n's builder community. Rather than rebuilding the brand from scratch, the system preserves recognizable elements such as its signature pink while creating more flexibility for an expanding product ecosystem.

item.title: Adobe Lightroom Mobile Can Now Open Closed Eyes in Photos with a Simple Tap (1 minute read)
item.description: Adobe's Lightroom mobile app now opens closed eyes with a single tap, surfacing an Open Eyes Quick Action whenever it detects closed eyes in a photo. Generative AI matches lighting and pose, drawing on other photos of the same person in the library, unlike Photoshop Elements, which borrows eyes from another shot. Free users get two tries before Adobe prompts them to subscribe to a Creative Cloud plan with more AI credits.

item.title: You can't hill climb your way to "good experience" (6 minute read)
item.description: Coding agents excel when success can be evaluated with deterministic tests, but good user experience cannot be reduced to a metric that can simply be optimized upward. Interfaces depend on nonlinear relationships between hierarchy, wording, context, attention, expectations, and human limitations, meaning hundreds of individually reasonable changes may still produce something confusing. AI can test whether an interface technically works, but its ability to read everything and perceive a whole page at once makes it a poor substitute for the distracted, imperfect humans who actually need to use it.

item.title: The New Age of Software (2 minute read)
item.description: Much software remains unbuilt for construction, manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, and healthcare administration, which still run on spreadsheets, paper forms, and systems installed around 1999. Best-paid designers and engineers went to social and ad networks, leaving industries too small, unsexy, or expensive for traditional software economics. Small teams can now build specialized tools in months and proofs of concept in days, and falling switching costs loosen vendor lock-in from legacy enterprise software.

item.title: How Meta Lets Designers Prototype with AI in Forum (1 minute read)
item.description: Meta's designers prototyped Forum, its standalone Facebook Groups app, with AI in a separate experimental build that used production components and excluded prototype code from release. The sandbox drew on the production codebase, frameworks, and design system, so approved work transferred without rebuilding from scratch. Agents ran build checks, automated tests, and visual comparisons before engineering review, and every shipped change required an engineer's approval.

item.title: Fast is a design decision (8 minute read)
item.description: AI has made websites dramatically easier to build, but generated experiences can still impose substantial costs on users through slow servers, excessive JavaScript, poorly prioritized media, ineffective caching, and other performance problems. Many of those costs originate in design decisions such as autoplaying video, multiple font weights, media-heavy carousels, and animations, making performance something designers should actively budget rather than leave entirely to engineers. Understanding a few fundamentals around rendering, CDNs, caching, loading priority, JavaScript, and real-world device performance lets designers and AI agents make deliberate tradeoffs between visual ambition and speed.

item.title: Sunlife's new logo design is "optimized for a digital world", but does it take minimalism too far? (4 minute read)
item.description: Canadian financial services company Sunlife has dramatically simplified its 25-year-old identity, turning Sun Life into a single word and reducing its detailed sun symbol to a simple yellow disc. The redesign aims to create a more contemporary, consistent identity optimized for digital environments while reflecting the company's expansion beyond life insurance into health, asset management, and other services. Its extreme simplicity has renewed debate around branding minimalism, with the lighter serif wordmark retaining some distinction while the stripped-back symbol risks the homogeneity associated with “blanding.”

item.title: This Artist's Epic Pencil Art Has Made Him a Rising Star in Indie Comics (1 minute read)
item.description: Fábio Simão dos Santos, a freelance comic book penciler who has made a living as an artist since 2019, is a rising talent in US indie comics.

item.title: Paper Mono (4 minute read)
item.description: Paper Mono is a free, open-source variable monospace family with eight weights, 800 glyphs, support for 100+ languages, and features including coding ligatures, duospace characters, box-drawing symbols, narrow spaces, alternate arrows, and a slashed zero, designed to work across headlines, body text, interfaces, and code.

item.title: Tarn Leith's Hard-Surface Designs and Character Concepts Live at the Intersection of Science Fiction and Fantasy (1 minute read)
item.description: Tarn Leith, a freelance concept artist working as TJL Art, creates hard-surface designs and character concepts that sit between science fiction and fantasy.

item.title: iPhone Duo orders limited to two per customer as Apple tackles scalping (2 minute read)
item.description: Apple is limiting iPhone Duo purchases to two per customer across markets including the US, UK, Japan, and Spain after shipping dates quickly slipped into January 2027. The restriction applies regardless of configuration and appears designed to reduce scalping, with resellers already listing devices for more than $5,000. Purchase limits cannot eliminate organized scalping entirely, but they could make bulk buying more difficult and improve availability for regular customers.

item.title: Figma co-founder Dylan Field thinks MCP is not a perfect protocol (2 minute read)
item.description: Figma is adding 20 MCP partners even as co-founder Dylan Field argues that the protocol favors frontier AI labs and needs improvement. He says the company wants people to use their Figma data but must limit exposure to reduce potential abuse. Field also pointed to unequal sharing of context across platforms and said Figma plans to support the open-source tool Pi.

item.title: Bluesky Expands its AI-Powered Attie App to Let Anyone Build Websites, Games, and More (2 minute read)
item.description: Bluesky's experimental Attie platform now lets everyday users build websites, quizzes, games, and polls, experiences that previously only software developers could make. CEO Toni Schneider calls it "social vibe coding," with creations tied to ATProto identities and able to reach Bluesky's 47 million registered users. Support for private data, the top developer request, is in alpha with a rollout planned by year's end.

item.title: Top Accessibility Errors in Production and How to Avoid Them (10 minute read)
item.description: Almost 96% of the top million home pages fail at least one automated accessibility check, and the same errors have led WebAIM's report for seven years. Low contrast, missing alt text, unlabeled inputs, and empty links and buttons top the list, each fixable without a rebuild. Automated scans catch only about 30 to 40 percent of issues, so keyboard and screen reader testing still has to happen before release.

item.title: “You've already proof-tested the answer for years” (4 minute read)
item.description: A formal design degree is not necessarily required to build a successful creative career when years of experience, skills, self-study, and leadership already demonstrate professional ability. The 70-20-10 learning model suggests that most professional development comes from practical experience and relationships, with formal education accounting for a relatively small portion. Structured courses can still be valuable when they address a specific knowledge gap, build confidence, or support a desired career direction rather than simply validating an already proven career.

item.title: Pure UI in the Agentic Era (8 minute read)
item.description: Treating UI as a pure function of state lets developers see how a screen varies across roles, plans, billing statuses, and flags, which matters more now that agents take on front-end implementation work. In a worked example, an agent that tested only an owner account reported success on a delete action, yet viewers still saw the button despite a “View only” header. Rendering every state combination side by side exposes such gaps, so teams should make display-relevant state explicit and ask what an agent actually checked before merging.

Its forms draw on historical serif designs and expressive swash lettering while balancing expressive details with enough consistency for the styles to be mixed freely. The result gives designers multiple distinct textures without requiring them to leave a single coordinated type family.

item.title: Digital Accessibility Laws for UX Designers: Which Rules Apply to Your Products (9 minute read)
item.description: Following accessibility best practices doesn't guarantee legal compliance, and the rules differ across the US, UK, and EU. A four-question check covering market, provider, product type, and exemptions helps identify which of the ADA, Section 508, the European Accessibility Act, and UK laws may apply. Cases involving Domino's, Target, and Fashion Nova show the legal and commercial cost of ignoring them.

item.title: Does brand design have a longevity problem? (8 minute read)
item.description: Brands increasingly chase launch-day novelty and short-lived visual trends at the expense of accumulated recognition and long-term usefulness. Durable identities instead build on principles, flexible systems, typography, proportion, composition, and other foundational elements that can evolve without abandoning the equity they have accumulated. Longevity does not require brands to remain visually static, but to preserve their core ideas while adapting their expression to new contexts over decades.

item.title: The Hardest Part of Moving from UX to Hardware is Committing (6 minute read)
item.description: Hardware demands earlier commitment than software, since a released physical product can't be fixed with an update and design choices become costly to reverse.

item.title: No More Icons In Every Menu By Default (1 minute read)
item.description: Apple has reversed the icon-heavy menu design introduced with macOS Tahoe.

item.title: Microsoft Redesigns Photos for Windows 11 (1 minute read)
item.description: Microsoft's redesigned Photos for Windows 11 adds a new Gallery, Editor, and Viewer, rolling out first to Windows Insiders, with wider availability planned later in 2026. Gallery merges local, OneDrive, and iCloud photos with natural-language search, while the Editor groups tools into Crop, Enhance, Repair, and Stylize.

item.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says (3 minute read)
item.description: Replit's CEO initially said the AI coding platform had stopped working with Anthropic over cost, partnership, and performance, claiming ChatGPT now builds vibe-coded apps better. Insiders familiar with the partnership rejected that, with one saying it remains in place. Replit's site and posts show Anthropic models in use as recently as a few weeks ago. He later clarified that OpenAI is the default, while Claude remains available.

item.title: WhatsApp wants to make stickers louder and chats a little less cramped (3 minute read)
item.description: WhatsApp is testing sound stickers on Android that let users attach up to 10 seconds of recorded or existing audio to custom stickers, while video-based stickers can retain five seconds of their original sound. Another option removes the outline around custom stickers for a cleaner appearance. A redesigned two-line compose box is also being tested, separating the typing field from additional controls to create more space and accommodate future shortcuts.

item.title: Product Designer is No Longer a Job Description (8 minute read)
item.description: Product designer no longer describes a single job, so four attributes (Style, Strategy, Builder, and Operator) offer a shared vocabulary for candidates and hiring managers. Craft is the floor beneath all four. Most strong designers lead with one or two.

item.title: Where decisions live (4 minute read)
item.description: Giving different kinds of project information distinct homes makes both teams and AI agents better at distinguishing current decisions from outdated discussions and unfinished thinking. A simple system can keep chronological observations and evolving ideas in running notes while maintaining a separate dated decision log that records what is currently true without deleting previous decisions. AI makes large amounts of context searchable, but chronology and structure remain essential because a searchable mess is still a mess.

item.title: UX designers are not designing interfaces, they design personalities (12 minute read)
item.description: Digital products increasingly translate human behavior into metrics such as sleep scores, ratings, streaks, story points, and follower counts, which can gradually influence how people understand themselves and behave. These measurements expose only selected parts of reality, yet their apparent objectivity can give them greater authority than unmeasured experiences, relationships, and intuition. UX designers therefore shape more than interfaces and experiences: by deciding which metrics products emphasize, they influence how people perceive themselves and should deliberately leave room for realities that cannot be quantified.

item.title: Fulham F.C gets a brand refresh built on hand-rendered lettering found on the walls of its stadium (5 minute read)
item.description: Fulham F.C's refreshed identity by Music and F37 Foundry is built around FFC Original, a bespoke typeface inspired by hand-rendered lettering discovered inside Craven Cottage, London's oldest football stadium. Rather than placing historical references alongside a contemporary identity, the system uses the club's physical heritage as the source of its modern visual language. The typography now extends across matchday graphics, campaigns, retail, moving image, and a 2026/27 away-kit campaign inspired by the visual language of the 1990s.

item.title: WCAG 3: A Different Future for Accessibility (7 minute read)
item.description: WCAG 3, still a draft, is the first ground-up rebuild of the standard since 1999, proposing to replace binary pass/fail with a graded model where meeting core requirements is a floor. Bronze, silver, and gold levels would let organizations be recognized for going further. Accessibility laws point to WCAG, so the change must keep regulators able to adopt it.

item.title: Structure First: The Inverted Pyramid and Visual Organization (5 minute read)
item.description: The inverted pyramid makes web content easier to consume by putting the essential message first and progressively adding supporting detail, ensuring readers understand the key point even if they stop early. Individual paragraphs should similarly lead with their main idea, while descriptive headings, short paragraphs, lists, and selective emphasis provide visual entry points for people scanning rather than reading linearly. A useful test is whether someone can understand something meaningful from a page within five seconds without reading its body copy. AI-generated writing is particularly worth checking for conclusions buried beneath unnecessary setup.

item.title: UX Maps: Glossary (5 minute read)
item.description: NN/g's UX Maps glossary defines and distinguishes common mapping tools.

item.title: At ORGATEC 2026 Sihoo Introduces Self Adjusting Chairs Built to Boost Creative Work (3 minute read)
item.description: Sihoo's self-adjusting H300 Pro and Doro C300 Pro V2 chairs, which have lumbar support that adapts to posture shifts, will be shown at ORGATEC 2026 in Cologne.

item.title: Apple's App Store rules now explicitly ban AI nudify apps (4 minute read)
item.description: Apple has strengthened its App Store rules to explicitly address AI-generated nonconsensual intimate imagery and apps that digitally undress people. Developers must proactively moderate harmful user-generated content, while a clarified rule prohibits hiding functionality during review and enabling features such as nudification after approval. The changes follow months of criticism over harmful AI apps reaching the App Store and incidents involving tools such as Grok being used to create sexualized deepfakes.

item.title: Figma Opens Code Layers Beta, Adds Specs and a Backend for Make (2 minute read)
item.description: Figma Code Layers has entered open beta across plans, running interactive prototypes beside design frames, with generation and editing free on paid plans through November 4. Specs adds shared Markdown documents that pass requirements to AI agents through MCP, and a Payload integration gives Make a database, CMS, and admin interface. Rollouts differ: Guidelines is in open beta on paid plans, Code sources stays closed, and Payload reaches all plans over the coming weeks.

item.title: Apple calls iPhone Duo pre-order demand ‘extraordinary' as shipping dates slip (2 minute read)
item.description: Apple says iPhone Duo pre-order demand has been “nothing short of extraordinary,” with shipping estimates quickly slipping from October into January and even February in some countries. Limited initial supply appears to be amplifying the delays, while Apple says it is working to get devices to customers as quickly as possible and will continue accepting online orders. The shortages have already created a resale market, with scalpers listing pre-orders for prices as high as $10,000.

item.title: Use Feedback as Your Superpower: Learn, Improve, Shine (24 minute read)
item.description: Feedback is the lifeblood of great design, and how someone responds to it matters more than they might think. There are four types of feedback: positive, constructive, negative, and appreciation. Negative comments can be reframed by acknowledging emotions, separating self from work, and staying curious.

item.title: Design in the material you ship (6 minute read)
item.description: Digital designers should understand code as a material in the same way architects understand stone or steel, learning what it can do without necessarily mastering how to write it. AI increasingly handles implementation, making it practical to design and review working interfaces in code where responsive behavior, real data, loading states, accessibility, and failure conditions can be experienced rather than represented as static pictures. The valuable skill is therefore shifting from syntax toward understanding how software behaves, testing its limits, and judging whether the resulting product actually works for people.

item.title: Synthetic Users vs. Human Respondents: Same Conclusion, Less Variation (6 minute read)
item.description: A comparison of 120 synthetic respondents with 604 humans produced the same broad conclusion about terminology for UX work, but AI-generated responses showed dramatically less variation. Synthetic participants converged on roughly a dozen labels while humans produced more than 50, demonstrating a form of mode collapse that can erase unusual perspectives and differences between groups. Synthetic users may help generate hypotheses or identify broad patterns, but they cannot replace human research when unexpected responses, minority perspectives, or natural variation matter.

item.title: How Span Reimagined the Nature Museum Identity (4 minute read)
item.description: Span redesigned Chicago's Peggy Notebaert Nature Museum around the colors, forms, and character of native Illinois prairies, creating a warmer and more expressive identity for both casual visitors and scientific audiences. Tonka provides an organic wordmark, while New Atten, seven colors named after prairie flora, and an abstract mark that can read as a butterfly, flower, or cloud give the system its distinctive character. The mark can frame photography, become a repeating pattern, or function independently, allowing the identity to extend across the website, signage, campaigns, posters, and museum store.

item.title: Together gives Clusia a four-petal mark showing AI and people at work (6 minute read)
item.description: Together created Clusia's identity around a four-petal mark representing multiple people and AI systems working together inside the assurance platform, deliberately avoiding the robotic visual language common to AI companies. The petals become pixels in 3D illustrations, animate through product states, and combine with Die Grotesk, Vitruv Text, forest-inspired colors, and candid workplace photography to create a system that feels technological but distinctly human. Generative AI was used to explore illustration forms before they were rebuilt and refined in Cinema 4D, while the product itself uses a restrained version of the identity with green reserved for actions, statuses, and the animated mark.

item.title: What to Do When Brand Archetypes Don't Help You Write UX Copy (6 minute read)
item.description: Brand archetypes give a brand a cohesive personality but leave sentence-level UX copy open to interpretation.

item.description: Working as Color out of Place, Brett Keyes makes AI-assisted landscapes where calm scenes, like Rippling Reality's mountain lake, dissolve into patterns of color and line.

item.title: Google Play Redesign Adapts to Car Displays (1 minute read)
item.description: Google's redesigned Play Store for cars with Google built-in adapts to different display sizes and orientations, rolling out automatically over the coming weeks. Entertainment collections for parked use sit apart from driving-related options, and a left-side rail becomes a top bar in portrait. YouTube Premium subscribers get background audio when the car shifts into drive, and Firefox and STARZ join the lineup.

item.title: Adobe Software Dupe Maker Takes on Microsoft Office, Releasing Free Versions of Word, PowerPoint, and Excel (2 minute read)
item.description: A developer who used AI to recreate Adobe's creative apps in Rust as free, open-source tools is now taking on Microsoft Office. WordCraft, DeckCraft, and GridCraft arrive as free stand-ins for Word, PowerPoint, and Excel under the ArtCraft brand. Some subreddits removed posts over cybersecurity and ethics concerns about AI-generated code. Supporters frame the apps as a protest against Adobe's subscription tactics.

item.title: Opera Air gets a minimalist makeover with a focus on distraction-free browsing (2 minute read)
item.description: Opera Air has been redesigned around distraction-free browsing, using a cleaner interface that keeps additional tools hidden until they are needed. New wallpapers use open spaces, perspective, and natural textures that adapt to light and dark themes, while built-in Soundscapes combine ambient sounds and original music to encourage focus or relaxation. The browser also includes customizable break reminders, breathing exercises, neck stretches, an ad blocker, and a free VPN while allowing messaging and social apps to remain accessible through the sidebar.

item.title: Critique in the AI Era (6 minute read)
item.description: AI can produce twelve credible variations before the coffee cools, so the design crit should become a debrief, like an F1 team studying telemetry over finishing position. Teams ask about reasoning, friction with the model and verification, and also critique the setup: briefs, constraints, and rubrics. AI critics tend to agree with the designer, and great AI-first designers sense limits, give precise feedback, and know when to override the model.

item.title: Scaling the Design Process (1 minute read)
item.description: Static personas capture real-world complexity poorly in intelligence-driven products, where outcomes are probabilistic and vary across people and contexts. AI lets teams build products that adapt to individual users at scale, which means designing for a spectrum of outcomes.

item.title: Agentic Systems Are the Future of Brands (8 minute read)
item.description: Traditional brand guidelines struggle when teams and AI agents must constantly make decisions that were never explicitly documented, causing otherwise competent work to gradually drift toward generic outcomes. Agentic brand systems can instead encode decisions about voice, color, typography, layout, components, and behavior into structured, machine-readable instructions that both humans and agents can apply directly. As AI dramatically increases the volume and speed of production, documenting not just what a brand looks like but why and how its decisions should be made becomes essential for maintaining coherence.

item.description: Studio Herrström's identity for Sony Music imprint Milkshake combines references from car culture, flavored drinks, and pop music into a single energetic visual language. The original splash mark has been redrawn as a rounded emblem inspired by fluid, metal, and reflections, accompanied by neon pinks, high-vis yellows, asphalt blacks, soft lilacs, and the neo-grotesque Gates typeface. Information layouts borrow from car window permits and milk carton nutrition tables, creating structured containers for track titles, release dates, copyright information, and other details across digital and promotional materials.

item.title: Fit height to background pattern size with calc-size() (4 minute read)
item.description: CSS background patterns can end awkwardly when a container's content produces a height that isn't an exact multiple of the background tile, while `background-repeat: round` fixes the edge by distorting the pattern itself. Combining `calc-size()` with `round()` instead lets the browser calculate the element's natural height and round it up to the nearest multiple of the tile height. The result behaves similarly to `min-height`, preserving both the content-driven size and the original pattern proportions, though browser support remains limited.

item.title: How to Turn an AI-Generated Logo into a Professional Logo (10 minute read)
item.description: AI-generated logos work as starting concepts, not finished brand assets, and need real editing before professional use.

item.title: How Any Designer Can Build a More Open Design Culture at Work (5 minute read)
item.description: Designers at any level can build a more open design culture by creating psychological safety one conversation at a time.

item.title: Getty Images to go private after restructuring deal (1 minute read)
item.description: Getty Images is planning a prepackaged Chapter 11 filing and will go private, backed by up to $533 million from the Getty family and Koch Equity Development. The deal follows a collapsed $3.7 billion Shutterstock merger and leaves the company, carrying over $1.3 billion in debt, wholly family- and Koch-owned. Generative AI image tools keep squeezing the stock-licensing business of both Getty and Shutterstock.

item.title: AI Agent Developer Manus Raises $500M+ at Reported $4B Valuation (2 minute read)
item.description: Manus has raised more than $500 million in a round led by Boyu Capital, with Tencent participating, at a reported $4 billion valuation. That figure roughly doubles Meta's reported offer, an acquisition Chinese regulators blocked in April. The newly released Manus 2.0 cuts token use by 23.2% on some tasks and adds Cloud Computer and Cue.

item.title: iOS 27.2 beta 4 removes Apple's redesigned Health app and brings back the old design (2 minute read)
item.description: Apple has removed its redesigned Health app from iOS 27.2 beta 4, restoring the existing interface after allowing testers to try the overhaul in earlier betas. The redesign introduced features including Insights, Longevity, Health Age, and readiness metrics, but Apple had already indicated that it would arrive separately later in 2026. Data collected while testing the new version remains available through Settings, suggesting the redesign has been delayed rather than abandoned.

item.title: On what a clean interface hides (5 minute read)
item.description: Minimal interfaces can reduce visible complexity while quietly transferring more work to users, who must discover hidden controls, interpret ambiguous icons, and infer what happened after an action. Comparing a hidden bookmark icon with an explicit Save button demonstrates how adding labels, confirmation, and an Undo action can make an interface visually busier but cognitively simpler. Good interface design therefore requires balancing visual restraint with enough visible information to support newcomers, while potentially reducing that guidance as familiarity grows.

item.title: Emerging Patterns: Design Leadership in 2026 (15 minute read)
item.description: Research involving 119 design leaders found 93 distinct routes into the profession, with fewer than 30% having studied in dedicated design programs and nearly 40% beginning their careers elsewhere. Traditional career ladders are giving way to more diversified portfolio careers, while 94% of respondents expect their tool stacks to change dramatically over the next five years as AI transforms design work. The qualities that appear most durable amid this uncertainty are not technical skills but intuition, navigation, adaptability, resilience, and stewardship, including a growing commitment among established designers to mentor the next generation.

item.title: When code is no longer the constraint: Inside Anthropic's design team (12 minute read)
item.description: AI has accelerated engineering at Anthropic to the point where deciding what deserves to be built is becoming a greater constraint than implementing it, pushing designers closer to production code and working prototypes. Designers routinely build their own tools, generate interactive variations using Anthropic's design system, and collaborate through smaller, more frequent critiques and working demos rather than lengthy specifications. Technical fluency is increasingly useful, but Anthropic also values designers who continually reinvent their workflows, have a point of view about where software is heading, and can move fluidly between strategic direction and hands-on making.

item.description: Open Source UI components built on a design philosophy where every animation serves a functional purpose — motion is information, not decoration.

item.title: Build Your Own Design Apps with AI (Website)
item.description: Toolcraft is an open-source starter kit and UI library for building custom design apps with AI. Use it to create branded asset generators, explore new visual styles, and turn repetitive design tasks into reusable tools.

item.title: Thumbnails Give a Fast Overview (15 minute read)
item.description: Thumbnails let people choose by looking rather than reading, because a scene's gist registers in about a tenth of a second. They fail when neighbors look identical or a preview misrepresents the click, so the two rules are: differ from your neighbors, and resemble your destination. Fourteen guidelines follow, along with the risks AI brings when it selects, personalizes, or synthesizes previews.

item.title: Experience Planes – The Big 4: Who, What, Where, and Why of Experiences (10 minute read)
item.description: Picking a single lens such as customer, shopping, or brand experience quietly shapes a design conversation before any design begins. Four experience planes widen the view: who is involved, what they are doing, where it happens, and why the organization offers it. Five examples, from license renewal to food delivery, show frustration often sitting in the connections between places.

item.title: How two simple dots gave Pictoplasma a fresh personality for 2026 (7 minute read)
item.description: andstudio transformed Pictoplasma's deliberately neutral identity around the positioning “Never faceless,” giving the character-design festival its own personality without competing with the work it showcases. A customized version of Lift Type's Melun adds a glyph containing two dots that function as eyes, allowing typography itself to become a character through pareidolia while colors and layouts change between festival editions. The same two-dot device extends into motion, print, installations, tattoos, and guerrilla applications, creating a playful system simple enough to work within the festival's limited budget.

item.title: André Britz draws dimly remembered landscapes, in a book held together with a pink elastic band (5 minute read)
item.description: André Britz's Gone with the Clouds collects intuitive landscapes drawn entirely from memory in a 64-page publication whose loose pages and pink elastic binding deliberately remain changeable, mirroring how memories blur, shift, and rearrange themselves over time.

item.title: The chaotic Apple HomeView ad is stressful viewing (4 minute read)
item.description: Apple's HomeView launch ad depicts a chaotic family morning, with the shared smart-home display handling messages, entertainment, and home controls.

This means that the differences that matter don't show up on a features page. item.title: As They Supposedly Battle AI Slop, Major Publishers Reportedly Cover Their Books in It (2 minute read)
item.description: Three of the big five publishers reportedly use AI for cover art and publicity copy without telling authors or the public. Wired's report, drawn from more than two dozen anonymous employees, names tools including ChatGPT, Claude, and image generators. Leadership subscribes to AI tools and runs brainstorming sessions asking staff to find uses, even as the big five sue Meta over copyright.

item.title: Prize-Winning Image Which Sparked Backlash Was AI-Generated, Nikon Rules (2 minute read)
item.description: Nikon has disqualified the winning video of its Small World in Motion microscopy contest, ruling that generative AI used in its composition broke the rules. Scientists, including former judges, had flagged the footage of cilia in a child's airway as fake. The camera-maker is now reviewing the procedures of the annual contest, which has run for 15 years.

item.title: Facebook is giving users more control over their algorithm (2 minute read)
item.description: Facebook's new “Your Algorithm” feature lets users describe in their own words what they want to see more or less of in Feed and Reels, with Meta saying recommendations update in real time. An updated three-dot menu provides access to the tool alongside “Interested” and “Not interested” options, and Facebook may ask follow-up questions to understand users' feedback. The launch brings controls already introduced on Instagram to Facebook, giving users a more direct way to shape their recommendations.

item.title: The Fake Double Diamond is Dead. The Real Double Diamond is Immortal (6 minute read)
item.description: Synthetic users and AI-generated insights offer the false certainty of up-front discovery without its substance, and they never remove the need to iterate. Shipping everything and letting analytics decide fails too, because real experiments need a hypothesis, an end point, and cleanup of failed bets. The fake double diamond trades real divergence for synthetic urgency. Useful software needs problem definition and iteration in one shared system.

item.title: What are we willing to sacrifice for AI? (7 minute read)
item.description: If AI eventually allows companies to produce goods and services with far fewer workers, economies built around exchanging labor for income may face a fundamental contradiction. Three broad responses each demand a sacrifice: businesses could preserve jobs at the expense of potential profits, society could restrict AI and forgo some of its benefits, or economic systems could provide guaranteed income or broader ownership while accepting greater institutional dependence. The deeper question is whether existing ideas about liberty and economic independence can survive if meaningful opportunities to earn a living through work become scarce.

item.title: TypeType Unveils TT Rationalist Typography (3 minute read)
item.description: TypeType's updated TT Rationalist modernizes the slab serif with trapezoidal serifs, softer stroke contrast, humanist proportions, and curved details that make dense text feel less rigid and more comfortable to read. The family spans 22 styles, including ten upright weights, matching true italics, and two variable fonts, with 1,127 glyphs per style and 31 OpenType features. Support for more than 235 Latin- and Cyrillic-based languages makes the family flexible enough for everything from editorial layouts and cultural posters to apps, watch interfaces, and compact digital typography.

item.title: Fix the Contrast without Losing Your Brand (3 minute read)
item.description: Low-contrast text appears on 83.9% of the top million home pages, making it the web's most common accessibility failure. Clearleft's tool “This hue shall pass” maps every pairing in a palette against WCAG AA or AAA and fixes failures by nudging lightness. Hue stays fixed, so brand colors keep their character while passing contrast.

item.title: Pentagram creates dynamic bilingual identity for Design Doha Biennial 2026 (4 minute read)
item.description: Pentagram's identity for the 2026 Design Doha Biennial replaces a static logo with a flexible typographic system built around connectivity and equal treatment of Arabic and English. Extended strokes stretch between elements like mapping lines or network constellations, while regional travertine beige and deep maroon are combined with bright orange and the blue established by the inaugural edition. The same structural logic extends across sub-brands and exhibitions, allowing individual programs to develop distinct expressions while remaining part of a coherent bilingual system.

item.title: A' Design Award Winners Achieve Real World Impact through Graphic Design (6 minute read)
item.description: A curated selection of 2026 A' Design Award winners shows graphic design and packaging delivering real-world impact, including Gold winners Aisling Sans and Dotline Corporate Identity.

item.title: The Best Way to Use Icons in Web UIs (18 minute read)
item.description: Icons can be inserted and swapped from CSS alone by storing them as custom-property design tokens and rendering them through masked pseudo-elements.
